title: With Due Respect (Vol. 3) -- Ch. 1: Mediation: A Useful Tool to Unclog Dockets
keywords: Mediation: A Useful Tool to Unclog Dockets
its Action Program for Judicial Reform
primary_topics: Chapter 1 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 3) -- CJP's May 27, 2007 Inquirer column promoting mediation as a tool to unclog court dockets, set against a crisis of fewer than 2,000 judges saddled with about a million pending cases (over 500 each)

Mediation's advantages over full-blown litigation -- speedy, peaceful, less expensive, 'win-win,' and suited to 'the Filipino way of ending problems sans loss of face' -- versus litigation that is 'tedious, time-consuming, stressful, expensive' and breeds 'broken relationships' and 'new cycles of violence'

How the Supreme Court, through the Action Program for Judicial Reform (APJR), piloted and then institutionalized court-annexed mediation -- training mediators through the Philippine Judicial Academy, creating the Philippine Mediation Center, and making mediation a mandatory part of pretrial

The 'phase two' Judicial Dispute Resolution (JDR) innovation (judges as conciliators/neutral evaluators), the emergence of accredited mediators as 'a new profession,' and the program's striking results (a 71-percent settlement rate across 35,223 cases mediated from 2002 to 2006)
sub_topics: The docket crisis: fewer than 2,000 judges carry about a million pending cases (averaging over 500 each, unevenly distributed -- some with 6,000, some with 200), worsening daily from new filings, with even a lower-court judgment often merely shifting the burden to an appellate court

The APJR toolkit: getting more judges appointed, making them work harder, computerizing the system, streamlining the Rules of Court, and promoting alternative dispute resolution (ADR) -- of which CJP focuses on mediation

Litigation's disadvantages: 'tedious, time-consuming, stressful, expensive,' often ending in 'broken relationships and permanent animosities,' sometimes inflicting 'deeper social wounds' and engendering 'vengeance as well as new cycles of violence'

Mediation's 'win-win' virtues: speedy, convenient, peaceful and cheaper; less confrontational and so suited to 'the Filipino way of ending problems sans loss of face'; able to improve relationships; usable before or during litigation -- an ancient technique once 'frowned upon' for ousting courts of jurisdiction, now welcomed in the e-age

The 2001 pilot: the Court asked the Philippine Judicial Academy (Philja) to train about 400 mediators who, working on actual cases in the NCR, Cebu and Davao, settled '80 percent of the 1,000 cases referred to them' in under two weeks -- some more than 10 years old

Institutionalization: court-annexed/referred mediation became a docket-decongestion tool, with a Philja curriculum, the Philippine Mediation Center (PMC) and its nationwide units, a mediation fee on every new case, and mandatory mediation at pretrial except for 'non-mediatable' cases

Phase two -- Judicial Dispute Resolution (JDR): piloted in the San Fernando (Pampanga) and Bacolod RTCs (an innovation from the National Judicial Institute of Canada), in which the pretrial 'JDR judge' acts as conciliator and 'neutral evaluator' to revive a failed mediation; if it still fails, the case is re-raffled to a new trial judge, with JDR offers and admissions inadmissible and the JDR judge barred from discussing them -- pioneered by Executive Judge Adelaida Ala-Medina

Mediation as 'a new profession': mediators are screened and trained by Philja, complete an internship, are accredited by the Court, need a four-year bachelor's degree (not necessarily a law degree), and are deemed 'officers of the courts' -- capped by the November 27-28, 2006 National Conference on Court-Annexed ADR Mechanisms (funded by USAID and The Asia Foundation), which reported a 71-percent settlement rate across 35,223 cases mediated from 2002 to October 2006

stances.claim: With fewer than 2,000 judges carrying about a million cases, litigation alone cannot move 'the wheels of justice' -- so the Court must promote alternative dispute resolution, above all mediation, to decongest dockets and let judges focus on cases 'that can neither be mediated nor compromised.'
stances.rhetorical_move: problem-and-solution framing: quantifying the backlog to justify a turn toward ADR

stances.claim: Mediation is superior to full-blown litigation for most disputes -- speedy, cheap, peaceful and 'win-win,' suited to 'the Filipino way of ending problems sans loss of face' -- and the pilot results prove it (80 percent of 1,000 cases settled in under two weeks; a 71-percent rate over 35,223 cases).
stances.rhetorical_move: comparative advantage plus evidence: contrasting litigation's harms with mediation's benefits and citing hard settlement data

stances.claim: The Court has rightly institutionalized court-annexed mediation and the JDR 'phase two,' turning mediation into an accredited profession of court 'officers' -- a durable structural reform, not a one-off experiment.
stances.rhetorical_move: institutionalization narrative: tracing the pilot's growth into permanent machinery

notable_anecdotes: Over 500 cases per judge: CJP opens with the arithmetic of crisis -- fewer than 2,000 judges and about a million pending cases, some judges buried under 6,000 -- to frame why reform is urgent.
'Voila!' in two weeks: he recounts the 2001 pilot in which trained mediators settled 80 percent of 1,000 referred cases -- some more than a decade old -- in less than two weeks.

The Canadian JDR import: he credits the National Judicial Institute of Canada for the 'phase two' Judicial Dispute Resolution model and names Executive Judge Adelaida Ala-Medina of San Fernando as a knowledgeable pioneer.

His farewell conference: he notes convening, just before retiring as CJ, the November 2006 National Conference on Court-Annexed ADR Mechanisms (USAID- and Asia Foundation-funded), which reported a 71-percent settlement rate across 35,223 cases.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 1 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 3), CJP's May 27, 2007 Inquirer column, makes the case for mediation as a tool to unclog court dockets, opening with a crisis: fewer than 2,000 judges carry about a million pending cases -- over 500 each, unevenly spread, some buried under 6,000 -- and the backlog worsens daily as new filings outpace judgments that often merely shift the burden to appellate courts. Through its Action Program for Judicial Reform (APJR), he writes, the Court is appointing more judges, computerizing, streamlining the Rules of Court and promoting alternative dispute resolution, of which he singles out mediation. Full-blown litigation is 'tedious, time-consuming, stressful, expensive,' breeding 'broken relationships' and even 'new cycles of violence'; mediation, by contrast, is speedy, peaceful, cheaper and 'win-win,' suited to 'the Filipino way of ending problems sans loss of face,' and usable before or during a case. Once 'frowned upon' for ousting courts of jurisdiction, mediation proved itself in a 2001 pilot in which Philja-trained mediators settled '80 percent of the 1,000 cases referred to them' in under two weeks -- some more than 10 years old -- prompting the Court to institutionalize court-annexed mediation, with a Philja curriculum, the nationwide Philippine Mediation Center, a per-case mediation fee, and mandatory mediation at pretrial (save 'non-mediatable' cases). A 'phase two,' Judicial Dispute Resolution (JDR) -- an innovation from the National Judicial Institute of Canada, piloted in the San Fernando and Bacolod RTCs and pioneered by Executive Judge Adelaida Ala-Medina -- lets the pretrial judge act as conciliator and 'neutral evaluator,' with strict confidentiality if it fails and the case is re-raffled. Mediation has become 'a new profession' of accredited court 'officers,' and CJP closes by recalling the November 2006 National Conference on Court-Annexed ADR Mechanisms (USAID- and Asia Foundation-funded), which reported settling about 24,983 of 35,223 cases mediated from 2002 to 2006 -- a 71-percent success rate.
